record.label: Bounded odd trigonometric angle approximation
record.statement: For any fixed finite descendant calculation with odd smooth local maps of polynomial derivative growth, and any η>0, the clipped output m*=clip(z) admits a finite bounded odd angle θ such that ‖sin(2θ)−m*‖<η. All sent columns can be bounded and odd; all pointwise maps can be finite real trigonometric sums with bounded derivatives.
record.boundary: The proof first fixes outer Lipschitz constants, then inner errors, using seed truncation, the regularized inverse sine, cutoffs and Fourier approximation. Approximation is in the rooted L² norm, not merely in marginal distribution.

aligned_passages.text: ### 8.2 Finite regularisation and the calculus needed for compilation Fix $T,N$ first. The independent continuous rounding coordinate makes the event at the sign discontinuity null. Bounded continuous odd approximations to that sign therefore converge in $L^2$ by dominated convergence. If the bounded output is $m^*$, shrink it to $(1-\kappa)m^*$, with fixed $0<\kappa<1$, before taking $\theta_\kappa=\tfrac12\arcsin((1-\kappa)m^*)$. This margin keeps the derivative of inverse sine bounded on its used range; the output loss is at most $\kappa$ in $L^2$. Then truncate the transmitted functions and approximate the resulting bounded maps by trigonometric polynomials. The source makes these choices from output toward leaves: each outer Lipschitz function is fixed before its inputs are approximated. The Gaussian isometry above converts an error in a transmitted child vector into the same $L^2$ error in its receiving position. Energy continuity then bounds the accumulated loss. The bounded output has the form $m=\sin(2\theta)$; it is the transmitted columns that are bounded, while the Gaussian fields themselves remain unbounded. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, bounded trigonometric approximation][q-bounded-classical]. **The formulas to be synthesized.** A mask is an event in the local seed space invariant under seed reversal. Fix a finite partition into masks, and write $p_R$ for the probability of mask $R$; probabilities used as denominators are positive. For disjoint masks $R,S$, aggregation on the finite regular tree means $$ (A_{RS}f)_i=\mathbf1_R(i)D^{-1/2} \sum_{j\sim i}\mathbf1_S(j)f_j. $$ A formula has a finite expression tree, with bounded measurable functions of the local seed as leaves. Internal operations are such aggregations or pointwise functions of previously formed quantities. Pointwise functions are smooth in their aggregate arguments, with polynomial bounds on all derivatives, uniformly in the seed. Seed dependence itself need not be smooth. Transmitted quantities are odd under simultaneous seed reversal; sent nonlinear functions and output angles are bounded, while aggregate Gaussian fields may be unbounded. An aggregation from $S$ to $R$ excludes $R$ if its transmitted formula uses no vertex of type $R$ below that call. All ancestor exclusions are retained, so a mask cannot recur on one active expression branch. It may recur on a different branch, and distinct branches may share descendants; exclusion asserts no independence between them. Gate targets are likewise excluded from the cross-edge dependencies of their parameters. This makes the physical all-neighbour calculation agree with the intended descendant calculation. For synthesis, reserve disjoint helper masks of positive mass, one per positive aggregation depth, absent from the output dependencies; the bounded odd output angle vanishes on their union. [OpenAI (2026b), Definition 3.3][q-formula-definition]; [Theorem 4.1][q-synthesis-statement]. The types can be encoded together with a Gaussian seed in one raw Gaussian variable: its sign supplies the odd symmetry, while disjoint binary digits of a uniform transform of its absolute value supply independent coordinates. The resulting finite type label is even and the Gaussian seed is odd under reversal. The associated pullback preserves vacuum, parity and $\mathsf L$. Thus adding types preserves the energy identification, rather than assuming an additional circuit resource. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, colours, exclusions and helpers][q-colors]. For the already fixed formula, the exclusion estimate is $$ \|m^{\rm col}-m\|^2\le C(\alpha+p_H), $$ where $\alpha$ is the largest nonhelper type mass and $p_H$ is the total helper mass. Its constant is independent of the number of types. The proof uses orthogonality of the disjoint masks before applying the Lipschitz estimate in the original, fixed list of formula coordinates. Treating the refined types as an arbitrary growing list of independent arguments would not provide this bound. The resulting classical near-optimality proposition supplies a finite bounded odd formula, zero on helpers, with energy as close to $P_*$ as required. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, “Type exclusion at small cost” and “Classical near-optimality in synthesis form”][q-colors]. **Which convergence permits the later substitutions?** The gate calculus uses recursive weights $\mathsf W_{h+1}=\mathsf W_0+d\Gamma(\Lambda_h)$, where $\Lambda_h$ is the previous weight restricted to the centred child space. The local weight includes the unbounded raw seed when needed. Its smooth domain is the intersection of all weighted domains. Smooth bounds mean polynomial bounds, with a finite loss of weight powers, for the maps, their adjoints and every specified parameter derivative. The finite height, fixed expression and fixed number of channels matter in these estimates. Strong convergence together with uniform stronger weighted bounds gives convergence in each weaker weighted norm by a spectral cutoff. This is the topology in which one replaces a gate inside a fixed surrounding circuit. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, weights and the topology of convergence][q-weights]. More precisely, the imported smooth-convergence contract is: for each output power $m$ and parameter multi-index $\alpha$, there are an input power $r$, exponent $k$ and constant $C$ such that $$ \|\mathsf W_D^m\partial_x^\alpha F_D(x)\xi\| \le C(1+|x|)^k\|\mathsf W_D^r\xi\|, \qquad \xi\in\bigcap_{q\ge0}\operatorname{Dom}(\mathsf W_D^q). $$ The bound is uniform in degree $D$ and parameter $x$. The same bound and strong convergence on smooth inputs are required for the adjoints and all specified parameter derivatives, with compatible limiting adjoints. Constants may depend on the fixed expression, height, channel list and derivative order. Bounded adjoint derivatives alone do not supply their convergence. At bounded local seeds $\mathsf W_0=1$; for polynomial Gaussian growth the source uses the vacuum-preserving weight $P_0+Q_0(1+|s|)Q_0$, where $P_0$ projects to the local vacuum and $Q_0=1-P_0$. These recursive weights control every generation. They differ from the top-generation number weight in §8.4's packet argument. No uniformity in growing word length, vanishing helper mass or the later seed-removal parameter is implicit in this contract. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, smooth-family bound][q-weights]. One of the essential inputs retains a term beyond the Gaussian field. Let $K_D(x)$ be a smooth unitary family with $K_D(0)=1$, uniformly controlled derivatives and adjoint derivatives that converge smoothly in the stated weighted topology to those of a limiting family $K$, and centred first vacuum derivatives. Write $K_\alpha=\partial_\alpha K(0)=iT_\alpha$ and $K_{\alpha\lambda}=\partial_\alpha\partial_\lambda K(0)$. For a fixed finite parameter list $a$, the source proves $$ K_D(a/\sqrt D)^{\otimes D}\longrightarrow \exp\!\left\{ i\sum_\alpha a_\alpha q(T_\alpha\mathrm{vac}) +\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda}a_\alpha a_\lambda \left\langle K_{\alpha\lambda} +\tfrac12\{T_\alpha,T_\lambda\}\right\rangle_0 \right\}. $$ The second term is imaginary by unitarity. It survives because a second-order change of size $D^{-1}$ occurs in each of $D$ children. Its scalar coefficients become a possibly nonconstant controlled operator when commuting signals replace $a$. For example, $K(x)=e^{ix^2}$ has zero first derivative at zero but $K(a/\sqrt D)^D=e^{ia^2}$ exactly. Keeping only the first derivative would miss even this elementary contribution. The example explains why the term is necessary; the source's weighted product lemma supplies the general convergence and domain bounds. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Products of small unitaries”][q-unitary]. Commuting substitution is justified through a joint spectral calculus and Fourier estimates. It requires the physical control algebra, the self-adjoint signal operators and receiving seed to strongly commute, with joint exponential and weighted derivative bounds as stated in the source. This is stronger than a formal commutator identity on one domain. It does not require a nonsingular covariance matrix or an inverse Gram matrix. Exclusions establish that commuting algebra before a preceding circuit is conjugated through it; conjugation preserves commutation even when the signals share descendants. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Smooth commuting substitution”][q-substitution]. The exact cut recursion records the effect of such shared lower calculations. Let $y$ be the incoming boundary data, $V(y)$ the root matrix, and $m(y)$ its outgoing signals in the current frame. Factoring out the operations wholly inside each child gives $$ E^{[d]}(y)=V(y)\prod_{j\ \mathrm{child}} K_j^{[d-1]}(D^{-1/2}m(y)),\qquad K^{[d]}(y)=u^*E^{[d]}(0)^*E^{[d]}(y)u. $$ Every ratio $K^{[d]}$ equals one at zero. Nevertheless $m(0)$ generally does not vanish, because removing the parent input leaves the root's own signals. The actual zero-boundary root update is $u_{\rm new}=E^{[d]}(0)u$. It is not recovered by setting the entire ratio to one and discarding the baseline operation. Applying the unitary product lemma to this recursion, and then commuting substitution, is the source's smooth gate calculus. Its replacement statement covers a fixed finite surrounding sequence and its required parameter derivatives; it does not assert uniformity for arbitrary sequences whose length or channel count grows. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, smooth gate calculus and its cut recursion][q-gate-calculus].

### 5.3 A fixed QAOA circuit before the thermodynamic limit Let $\widehat Z_i,\widehat X_i$ be Pauli operators, and define the cost and mixer by $$ C_{n,J}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i0$ there is one finite $W$ with $v(W)\geq P_*-\varepsilon$, whose depth and angles depend on $\varepsilon$ but not on $n$ or $J$. The instance still determines $C_{n,J}$. Here depth counts global cost–mixer layers; their elementary gate counts depend on the implementation. This order of limits differs from the fixed-instance depth limit in [Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann, §VI][FGG], which permits instance-dependent choices. The common-circuit conclusion was conjectured by [Basso, Farhi, Marwaha, Villalonga and Zhou (2022), §7, equation (7.2)][BFMVZ]. **The finite Gaussian input.** Fix the minimiser and its diffusion, a cutoff $0[long §7, “A finite Gaussian spin and its adjacent correlations”](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-gaussian-approximation). **The rooted energy and its circuit realisation.** The next identity comes from a separate construction in [OpenAI (2026b), §2 and Lemma 3.1][Q]. Its classical sector consists of square-integrable functions built recursively from a local Gaussian seed and Gaussian coordinates generated by child functions; the inner product is expectation. Centred real child directions have lifts $\mathsf G(f)$ at the receiving root that form a centred Gaussian family with $$ \mathbb E[\mathsf G(f)\mathsf G(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle. $$ The receiving root's seed is independent of these coordinates. Compatible embeddings compare functions of different finite depths without changing earlier variables. The root shift $\mathsf L$ inserts a child direction into the first Gaussian chaos (the linear Gaussian part), with constant receiving-root state; its adjoint projects onto that part and returns the child direction. This representation builds on the fixed-depth spin–boson description of [Boulebnane et al. (2026)][spin-boson]. Start with the root seed $g_0$ and recursively put $Z_{j+1}=\mathsf G(g_j)$. The orthonormal child directions give independent standard Gaussian lifts, reproducing the scalar law. The finite spin $F_N$ depends only on those lifts. Projection therefore gives the exact rooted-energy identity $$ \begin{aligned} \mathsf L^*F_N&=\sum_{j=0}^N\mathbb E[F_NZ_{j+1}]g_j,\\ \mathcal E(F_N):=\operatorname{Re}\langle F_N,\mathsf L F_N\rangle &=\sum_{j=0}^N\mathbb E[F_Ng_j]\,\mathbb E[F_NZ_{j+1}] =S_{T,N}. \end{aligned} \tag{12} $$ Independence of the receiving-root seed removes the $j=0$ term. This identity concerns the finite Gaussian formula in a limiting rooted space, not a finite-$n$ circuit. The unshifted pairing can have the same scalar limit without identifying this energy. The construction and projection are proved in [long §8.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#rooted-energy). **Proposition 5 (circuit approximation; a consequence of [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–5][Q]).** For each fixed $T,N$ in the preceding construction with finite positive normalisers, and every $\eta>0$, there is a finite ordinary QAOA word $W$, with deterministic angles independent of $n$ and $J$, such that $$ |v(W)-S_{T,N}|<\eta. $$ This imports the circuit construction for these particular Gaussian data. Bounded smooth odd approximations to the transmitted functions, together with exclusions on dependencies between seed classes, make the formula eligible for Theorem 4.1 while changing its rooted energy arbitrarily little. Smoothing the final sign alone is insufficient. That theorem synthesises the formula with temporary Gaussian seed controls, reusing the same sitewise seeds throughout the word. Theorem 5.1 removes their joint effect using cost and mixer gates. Proposition 2.1 identifies the resulting fixed word's tree energy with $v(W)$. The absolute approximation bounds give Proposition 5; [long §§8.1–8.6](../long/reasoning-record.md#qaoa-construction) retain the eligibility conditions and proofs. The deduction of near-optimality is now explicit: $$ P_*-v(W)\leq (P_*-I_T)+|I_T-S_{T,N}|+|S_{T,N}-v(W)|. \tag{13} $$ Choose $T$ so that $1-T<\varepsilon/3$, then $N$ so that the second term is below $\varepsilon/3$, and finally use Proposition 5 with $\eta<\varepsilon/3$. These finite choices give $v(W)>P_*-\varepsilon$ before $n$ tends to infinity. The source's Appendix A supplies an alternative positive-temperature input to the same synthesis. The selected construction supplies no quantitative depth bound, finite-size rate or efficient procedure for finding angles. **Corollary 6 (a measured configuration on the same instance).** For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite ordinary QAOA word $W_\varepsilon$, chosen independently of $n$ and $J$, such that one computational-basis measurement $\Sigma$ satisfies $$ \Pr_{J,\Sigma}\!\left\{ \max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)-H_{n,J}(\Sigma)\leq\varepsilon n \right\}\longrightarrow1 \qquad(n\to\infty). \tag{14} $$ **Proof.** For a fixed word, put $Y_n=H_{n,J}(\Sigma)/n$ and $K_n=\max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)/n$. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou, §4, equations (13)–(22)][FGGZ] prove $$ \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}Y_n\to v(W),\qquad \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}Y_n^2\to v(W)^2. $$ The second moment is $\mathbb E_J\langle(C_{n,J}/n)^2\rangle$, so it includes measurement variance as well as disorder fluctuations. Thus $Y_n\to v(W)$ in joint $L^2$. Gaussian concentration of the maximum and its defining mean limit give $K_n\to P_*$ in probability. Choose $W$ with $P_*-v(W)<\varepsilon/3$. With probability tending to one, both $K_n-P_*<\varepsilon/3$ and $v(W)-Y_n<\varepsilon/3$, which proves (14). The two energies use the same $J$; no independence between them is needed. The companion's [§11.2, “What is averaged, and a fixed-word probability consequence”](../long/reasoning-record.md#fixed-word-probability) gives the concentration argument and its further probability consequences.
